beats.say: Everyday prices promise fairness. And they all look the same.
A catalog of everyday tags, no sales, just flat prices.
The same items cost the same every day, no coupons needed.
A premium line with higher tags, marketed as 'premium quality'.
Sales fell 25% that year. Sounds dramatic.
But it's a discount illusion, the 'fair' tag hides a reference point.
Customers compare every item to the premium line, feeling they're getting a deal.
The premium tags sit at $120, $90, $60, making the regular $80 feel cheap.
Result: sales tumble $985 million, and the board pulls the CEO.
You see it at a bakery: $4 loaf, $6 artisan loaf, $8 'gourmet' loaf.
The $6 loaf looks like a bargain against $8, even though it's still overpriced.
Consumers pick the middle, thinking they avoid overpaying.
If a price feels 'fair', check the higher reference. Follow for more.
